criticism.title: Is it true?
criticism.read:
After the meeting your manager said, “Your presentation was all over the place.” All evening that sentence kept turning in your head: you thought about how they said it, that they said it in front of everyone, that they themselves had actually come unprepared.

Marcus Aurelius writes to himself: if someone shows me I’m wrong, I’ll gladly change. Because I’m looking for the truth, and no one has ever been harmed by the truth; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their error.

When criticism comes, the first thing we usually ask is, “Who said it? How did they say it? What right do they have?” These aren’t unimportant, but they aren’t the first question. The first question is this: is it true? A true word can come from a rude mouth; and a false one from a polite mouth.

Someone panning for gold doesn’t turn away from a muddy river; they shake the pan, let the mud wash out, and keep what shines.

When you find the truth inside a criticism, it’s no longer an attack on you, but something given to you.
criticism.body: Write down a recent criticism you received. Set aside who said it and how, and ask only: what in it is true? Mark its share as a percentage.
criticism.ask: Did you find something true inside a criticism today? What did seeing it change?

criticism.title: My other faults
criticism.read:
Someone talked about you behind your back; a friend told you. You’re already building your reply: it wasn’t really like that, they’re not so innocent either, why would they say that?

Epictetus used to advise his students: if you hear that someone has spoken badly of you, don’t defend yourself. Just say, “Clearly they don’t know my other faults; otherwise they’d have mentioned those too.”

This isn’t putting yourself down. Someone who already knows they aren’t perfect isn’t shattered when one of their faults is named. Defending yourself, on the other hand, is like a wall: it protects you, but it also keeps you from hearing anything from the other side.

A stone thrown at a smiling face makes less noise than one that hits a stone wall.

When you let go of defending yourself, you don’t lose anything. You simply make room to listen.
criticism.body: Today, when you’re criticized, say “You might be right, let me think about it” before you reply. Leave the defense for later.
criticism.ask: What happened today when you put off defending yourself? What did you hear?

criticism.title: Unfair criticism
criticism.read:
It really was unfair. You were blamed for a mistake you didn’t make, or your work was belittled without anyone understanding it. There’s anger inside you, and a rush of “I have to set this straight.”

Epictetus reminds us: when someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you, they do it because it seems right to them. They can act by their own idea of what’s right, not by yours. If they’re mistaken, the one harmed isn’t you, but the one who is deceived.

This doesn’t mean giving in to injustice. If needed, you can calmly correct it and show your evidence. But you don’t have to carry their wrong judgment on your own back. A wrong map doesn’t change the road; it only gets the person carrying it lost.

A letter left at the wrong address isn’t yours, even if it’s on your doorstep.

Unfair criticism is their burden. You only carry how you respond.
criticism.body: Before you reply to a criticism you find unfair, write a single sentence from their point of view: “They saw it this way, because…”
criticism.ask: When you tried to see an unfair criticism through their eyes, what happened to your anger?

criticism.title: The teacher
criticism.read:
Asking for feedback is hard. When you ask, “What did you think?” you actually want to hear “I liked it”; you’re afraid of the real answer.

Marcus Aurelius opens the first book of his notes by thanking the people who taught him something. Of his teacher Rusticus he writes: from him I learned that my character needed correcting and training. The emperor of Rome counts the man who criticized him among his most valuable teachers.

We tend to think of criticism as something that happens to us. Yet the wise person doesn’t wait for it and endure it; they look for it. Because no one can see their own back; for that you need another pair of eyes.

A tailor can’t see the back of his own jacket; even in front of the mirror, someone else has to look.

Asking for criticism takes courage. But whoever asks for it has found themselves a teacher.
criticism.body: Ask someone you trust for honest feedback on something: “How could I do this better?” Listen to the answer without interrupting.
criticism.ask: What surprised you most in the feedback you asked for?

criticism.title: The inner critic
criticism.read:
No one said anything, but you’re saying it to yourself: “You blew it again. Why are you always like this?” At night in bed, the worst moment of the day plays over and over.

Every night, after the lamp was out, Seneca would review his day: which of my faults did I heal today, what mistake did I make? But at the end of his questioning he would tell himself: “Don’t do that again; this time I forgive you.”

The harshest critic is often not outside, but inside. People think beating themselves up is the same as improving themselves. It isn’t. Just as a child raised on fear doesn’t become better, a mind that is constantly scolded doesn’t heal; it only grows tired.

A good teacher points out the mistake, then touches the student’s shoulder.

You can look at yourself like a teacher too: honest, but kind.
criticism.body: In the evening, review your day the way Seneca did. Write three things: one mistake, one lesson from it, and one act of forgiving yourself.
criticism.ask: How did you talk to yourself today? Would you talk to a friend that way?

criticism.title: When you criticize
criticism.read:
Your teammate missed the deadline again. You need to say something, but either you’ll say it too harshly, or you won’t say it at all and let it build up inside.

Marcus writes to himself about what to do when someone makes a mistake: show them their error kindly, without mocking them, without hurting them. Just as a father might tell his child, “No, my dear, we weren’t made for this; it’s harming you.” And do it not in front of others, but one on one.

People think giving criticism means condemning the other person. It doesn’t. Good criticism looks at the behavior, not the person, and talks about the next step, not the past. Its aim isn’t to be proven right, but to do better together.

A skilled gardener isn’t angry at the tree when he prunes a branch; he only shows it where to grow from.

How you give criticism decides whether it will be heard.
criticism.body: Choose a criticism you need to voice. Say it at a calm moment, one on one, talking about a specific behavior, not the person.
criticism.ask: Did you give someone criticism today? How was it received, and how did you feel?

criticism.title: Being looked down on
criticism.read:
For a week you’ve been working with criticism. In some you found a share of truth, some you saw through the other person’s eyes, and maybe you asked someone for it yourself.

Marcus asks himself: will someone look down on me? That’s their business. Mine is not to do or say anything that deserves to be looked down on. Will they be angry with me? That’s their business too. I’ll stay kind and well-meaning toward everyone.

People think taking criticism means carrying everything that’s said inside you. The opposite: once the lesson has been taken from a criticism, the rest is let go. Whoever cracks the shell and takes what’s inside doesn’t carry the shell around in their pocket.

The hand that cracks hazelnuts drops the shells to the ground; only the kernels stay in its palm.

Your measure no longer lies in what others say. But you’re still open to learning from what they say.
criticism.body: Pick one of this week’s criticisms. Write the one lesson you’ll take from it in a single sentence; let the rest go on purpose.
criticism.ask: Over these seven days, how has the way you see criticism changed?
